alerts.title: Alerts
alerts.subtitle: Emotional state + actionable advice. We refer to professionals when critical.
alerts.proTitle: Critical alerts detected. You're not alone.
alerts.proDesc: If you notice signs of distress (isolation, self-harm, severe cyberbullying, suicidal ideation), reach out to a professional now. These resources are free and confidential:
alerts.howToTalk: How to talk about it with your kid
alerts.needHelpDesc: If signs persist or worsen, don't wait. Call the resource below — talking to an expert can change everything.

adv.night1: Tonight, charge the phone outside the bedroom. Without it nearby, sleep improves on its own.
adv.night2: Turn on grayscale from 9pm. It's boring by design — and that's exactly the point.
adv.night3: Put the charger in the hallway or living room this week. It's a change of location, not a fight.
adv.night4: Ask how they feel on mornings after bad sleep. Help them connect rest with their own energy and mood.
adv.social1: Agree a realistic daily limit for their favourite app together. 30-45 minutes is a good starting point.
adv.social2: Swap 10 minutes of screen time for 10 minutes of something physical: a walk, music, drawing.
adv.social3: Give them a 10-minute warning before screen time ends. No surprises means fewer battles.
adv.social4: Treat phone time as something earned, not something always available by default.
adv.burst1: When they feel the urge to pick up the phone, suggest waiting 5 minutes first. Training the pause works.
adv.burst2: Ask what they're looking for when they open it so many times. If it's boredom, find a concrete alternative together.
adv.burst3: Set up a rule in NSK to get an automatic alert when this happens. The data speaks for itself.
adv.forbidden1: Before setting a rule, ask what they were looking for in that app. Understanding the why changes the conversation.
adv.generic1: Wait 1-2 hours before talking. The moment of tension is never the best time to reach agreements.
adv.generic2: Ask how they feel, not how long they've been on the phone. Emotions open more doors than data.
adv.generic3: Agree on one small change this week. One rule kept is worth more than ten broken.
adv.generic4: Tell them when they do well. A 'you nailed it today' has more impact than any punishment.
adv.generic5: Be consistent rather than strict. One simple rule applied always beats many rules that get forgotten.

talk.preventive: I noticed something in the data and wanted to ask how you felt today with the phone. No anger, just curious.
talk.moderate: I want to understand what's going on this week. What does that app give you? How does it leave you after?
talk.critical: I'm here, no judgment. What matters is how YOU are. Want us to look for help together?

learn.title: Learning hub
learn.subtitle: Actionable micro-lessons for parents. Mark the ones you apply.

talk.title: How to talk to your kid about phone use
talk.body: Create a no-judgment space to talk about digital life without turning it into an interrogation.
steps: Pick a neutral moment (walk, car), never right after an alert.
Start by asking what they enjoy, not how long they spend.
Share one of your own bad habits first to build trust.
Agree together on one simple rule: screen-free zones or moments.
talk.tip: Avoid 'you're on your phone all day'. Replace with 'what does this app give you?'.

warning.title: Signs that something's not right with the phone
warning.body: There are patterns that warn you before the problem gets big. Learn to recognise them.
steps: Notice if they suddenly change mood right after using the phone.
Watch if they use the phone at night when they should be sleeping, or open it many times in a row.
Pay attention if they spend nearly all their time on one single app and get anxious when they can't use it.
If you see two or more of these signs in a week, it's time for a calm conversation.
warning.tip: NSK detects these patterns automatically and alerts you. You don't have to watch alone.

night.title: Night digital hygiene
night.body: Sleep is the first thing affected by digital use. Restoring it changes everything.
steps: No screens 60 minutes before sleep.
Charge the phone OUTSIDE the bedroom (golden rule).
Enable grayscale mode from 9pm.
Create a 7-day quest in Quests: 'Sleep without phone'.
night.tip: Blue light delays melatonin up to 90 minutes. The body does not 'get used to it'.

habits.title: Building healthy digital habits
habits.body: Better to design the environment than to rely on the kid's willpower.
steps: Remove non-essential notifications from the kid's phone.
Move social apps to a secondary folder, off the home screen.
Set family moments with all phones in a box.
Reinforce healthy days positively with points in Quests.
habits.tip: Children's brains learn by reinforcement. Reward presence, not absence.

dopamine.title: Why they can't stop scrolling
dopamine.body: TikTok, Reels and Shorts are designed so the brain doesn't want to stop. Understanding why helps you act.
steps: Explain that these apps work like a slot machine: you never know what comes next, and that's what hooks you.
Agree a daily time limit for that app together. 30-45 minutes is a good starting point.
Set up an alert in NSK so you get notified when they've spent too long on that app.
Swap 10 minutes of scrolling for 10 minutes of something real: going out, music, drawing, whatever they enjoy.
dopamine.tip: The problem isn't the app, it's the format. A long video entertains just as much and hooks far less.

compulsive.title: When the phone can't wait
compulsive.body: If your kid picks it up many times in a short while, the phone may be in charge — not them. Here's how to spot it and act.
steps: Notice if the first thing they do when waking up is check the phone, before even speaking.
Watch if they get anxious or moody when the phone isn't nearby or you take it.
NSK automatically detects if they open it more than 5 times in 10 minutes and alerts you.
Agree a simple rule together: the phone stays in a fixed spot between meals and at night.
compulsive.tip: Showing them the data together, calmly, usually opens a better conversation than any telling-off.

limits_broken.title: What to do when they exceed screen time
limits_broken.body: Exceeding the limit doesn't mean you've failed. It means it's time to talk, not punish.
steps: Don't act in the moment: wait for calm before talking.
Show them the data in NSK: 'today you've had X hours, we agreed Y'. Data is neutral — it doesn't accuse.
Ask what they were doing and how they feel when they have to stop.
Agree together what happens tomorrow. A small rule they helped make is worth more than a big one imposed.
limits_broken.tip: Kids respect limits they helped set far more than ones that arrive without warning.

boundaries.title: Setting limits without battles
boundaries.body: Limits are respected when understood, not when imposed.
steps: Explain the why — sleep, focus, more energy — not just the what.
Show them the NSK data. Talking with real numbers is harder to argue with.
Agree together what happens if the limit is broken, BEFORE it happens.
When they keep to it, say so. Recognition works better than punishment.
boundaries.tip: Firm and warm beats harsh or absent. Aim for firm and kind.

family_rules.title: Agreeing digital rules as a family
family_rules.body: Rules agreed together are kept far better than rules handed down from above.
steps: Get the family together in a calm moment and ask: what phone rules would make sense at home?
Write down everyone's suggestions, including the child's. Their opinion matters.
Agree on a maximum of 3 clear rules. A few clear ones beat many confusing ones.
Put them somewhere visible. Review every month and adjust what isn't working.
family_rules.tip: When the child helps create the rule, they feel ownership of it — and keep it far more.

night_routine.title: Creating a screen-free night routine
night_routine.body: What we do in the last hour before sleep determines how we sleep. Screens are the worst ending.
steps: Pick a phone cut-off time: 30-60 minutes before sleep is enough to start.
Replace that time with something calm: reading, soft music, a conversation, a shower.
Put the phone on charge outside the bedroom before the agreed time.
Do this for several days in a row. The body builds the habit in under two weeks.
night_routine.tip: A night routine is the most valuable habit there is. It improves sleep, mood and focus the next day.

screen_awareness.title: How much screen time is too much
screen_awareness.body: There's no magic number, but there are clear signs that use is affecting your child.
steps: Notice how they are after a lot of screen time: irritable, tired, unfocused?
Compare their screen time with their sleep, physical activity and family time.
Check in NSK how much time they've had this week. Objective data is more useful than gut feeling.
If digital time is overtaking the offline activities they enjoy, it's time to adjust.
screen_awareness.tip: The problem isn't the number of hours, it's the impact on their life. Watch the impact, not just the clock.

anxiety_digital.title: When the phone creates anxiety
anxiety_digital.body: The phone can relieve discomfort short-term, but it can also be the source of the problem.
steps: Notice if they use the phone to escape difficult situations: arguments, boredom, loneliness.
Check if they're more anxious on high-use days than low-use days.
NSK measures screen time and compulsive sessions. Together, these can signal the phone is being used to manage anxiety.
Talk without judging: ask what they feel when the phone isn't nearby.
anxiety_digital.tip: The phone doesn't create the anxiety, but it can maintain it. If the pattern repeats, consider speaking with a professional.

boredom.title: Boredom is not the enemy
boredom.body: When a child is bored and automatically reaches for the phone, they're missing the chance to learn to manage their own mind.
steps: Next time they say 'I'm bored', wait 10 minutes before letting them pick up the phone.
Keep a short list at home of things to do without a screen — so you don't have to invent it in the moment.
Normalise boredom: explain that the discomfort of not knowing what to do passes on its own, and that's when the best ideas appear.
Reinforce when they come up with something themselves. That's exactly what you want.
boredom.tip: Boredom is where creativity starts. Letting them sit with it for a few minutes is one of the best gifts you can give.

attention.title: Focus in the age of the phone
attention.body: Every notification interrupts the brain and it can take up to 20 minutes to fully refocus.
steps: When doing homework or reading, the phone must be in another room — not face-down on the desk.
Turn off notifications for non-urgent apps. Fewer notifications, more focus.
Try the block method: 25 minutes of work, 5 minutes of rest. Rest does NOT mean the phone.
If they struggle to focus, practise together with gradually longer stretches without interruptions.
attention.tip: Focus is a muscle. It's trained like any skill: with consistent practice and no interruptions.

morning_start.title: Starting the day without checking the phone
morning_start.body: The first thing we do when we wake up sets the brain's tone for the rest of the day.
steps: Agree that the first half hour of the day is phone-free for everyone — parents included.
Swap the phone alarm for a physical alarm clock and leave the phone charging in another room.
The first few days can be hard. That's normal. The brain takes a few days to adapt.
When they manage it for several days in a row, recognise it and add it as a quest in NSK.
morning_start.tip: Starting the day without notifications lowers stress from the very first moment. They notice it, and so do you.

weekend_screen.title: Weekends and screen time
weekend_screen.body: A weekend without clear rules can become the highest-use moment of the week.
steps: Agree a screen limit for the weekend — different from weekdays if needed, but it must exist.
Plan at least one offline family activity each weekend: an outing, a game, a visit.
If NSK detects a usage spike on Saturday or Sunday, use it as a calm conversation starter, not a blame.
Leave some room: the weekend is for rest, not for rigid schedules.
weekend_screen.tip: A weekend with more digital freedom doesn't ruin the week's habits — as long as there's a clear agreement in place.

ios.s1Title: Open the Shortcuts app on the kid's iPhone
ios.s1Body: It's the gray app with two colored shapes. Pre-installed on iOS. Tap + at the top right to create a new shortcut.
ios.s2Title: Scan the QR to set URL and token
ios.s2Body: Point the camera at the QR below. You'll get the URL and your kid's unique token, only used in this shortcut.
ios.s3Body: Method: POST · Header: Content-Type: application/json · Paste the JSON below as request body. Optional: add 'Get Screen Time' first (iOS 17+).
ios.s4Title: Schedule the shortcut and send the first signal
ios.s4Body: In Shortcuts → Automation → Time of Day, repeat every night at 23:00. Run the shortcut once now to send the first signal.

and.s1Title: Install Tasker or HTTP Shortcuts on the kid's Android
and.s1Body: Tasker (Play Store) or the free 'HTTP Request Shortcuts' app work great. Open it and create a new task/shortcut.
and.s2Title: Scan the QR to copy URL and token
and.s2Body: Point the Android camera at the QR. Paste the URL as POST target and the token in the JSON body.
and.s3Title: Set up the POST request with the JSON
and.s3Body: Method: POST · Header: Content-Type: application/json · Body: the JSON below. In Tasker, use the 'HTTP Request' action.
and.s4Body: In Tasker → Profiles → Time, set it daily at 23:00 (or whenever). Run once to send the first signal.

quick.title: Connect {{name}}'s phone in 30 seconds
quick.subtitle: The child scans the QR with the camera. No install needed. Works on iOS and Android.
quick.step1Title: The child opens the phone camera
quick.step1Body: No app to install. Just the normal camera. Point it at the QR code above.
quick.step2Title: Tap the link that appears on screen
quick.step2Body: The NeuroShield Kids screen opens in the browser. You'll see the green 'Connected' dot within seconds.
quick.step3Title: Save it to the home screen (optional but recommended)
quick.step3Body: On iPhone: tap Share → Add to Home Screen. On Android: accept the install prompt when it appears. This allows background monitoring too.
